newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish 2-yr, 5-yr fixed bond prices seen easing.
newsitem.headline: Polish 2-yr, 5-yr fixed bond prices seen easing.

text.p: Prices of Poland's 16-percent two-year and 12-percent five-year bonds are expected to ease at Thursday's joint 800 million zloty tender, analysts said.

They said investors were likely to test higher yields mainly because of uncertainty over the possible interest rate rise in the near future, which could make players willing to gamble for lower prices.
"Considering the central bank's statements about a possible interest rates rise, it seems yields of the bonds may rise," said Marta Moscinska from Bank Slaski SA.

Thursday's Gazeta Wyborcza daily quoted the National Bank of Poland's president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz as saying that the bank would consider an interest rate rise in January to curb fast growing credit action.
Analysts expected maximum yields of the two-year paper, maturing February 12, 1999, to inch up to 20.40 percent from 20.30 percent at the last fixed bond auction on November 21.
The maximum yield of the five-year paper, maturing in February 12, 2002, was expected to rise by about 0.1 point from 18.15 percent at the last primary auction. @

They expected the auction will be undersubscribed, just like recent primary T-bill auctions, with demand focused on the shorter paper and not exceeding a total of 600 million zlotys against the treasury's 800 million offer.
"The disproportion between demand for two- and five-year papers will remain with greater interest in shorter bonds," said BSK's Moscinska.

Dealers expected, however, that the finance ministry would sacrifice a part of investor demand to limit price falls, as its liquidity needs in December were satisfied by big demand for one- and three-year bonds from individuals. @
Individual investors increased bonds purchases in December, because such investment was tax-deductable.
"The finance ministry may easily reject some 100 to 200 million zlotys worth of bids on Thursday to protect prices," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski from ING Bank in Warsaw.

Analysts said secondary bids for five-year bonds at yields of 19.50 percent signalled there was small buying interest, but they said demand could come from insurance companies keen on matching bond maturity with longer liabilities.
Foreigners were expected to bid only for small amounts of the shorter papers, and not interested in the five years bonds. @
The settlement date of the shorter paper is January 5, 1997 and January 12, 1997 for the longer bond.
